title: Microsoft, Google, xAI Open AI Models to U.S. Government for National Security Vetting
summary: Three of the most powerful tech companies in the world are handing over their latest artificial intelligence models to the U.S. government for security screening before public release. Microsoft, Google, and Elon Musk's xAI announced the agreement with the Commerce Department's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) on Tuesday, amid escalating fears that cutting-edge AI could supercharge cyberattacks or be exploited by adversaries. The deal fulfills a July pledge by the Trump administration to partner with industry to vet AI for 'national security risks.' Under the arrangement, government scientists will probe the models for unexpected behaviors and develop shared testing protocols. 'Independent, rigorous measurement science is essential to understanding frontier AI and its national security implications,' said CAISI Director Chris Fall. The move comes just days after the Pentagon revealed a separate agreement with seven tech giants—including Microsoft, Google, and SpaceX—to integrate AI into classified military networks, aiming to 'augment warfighter decision-making in complex operational environments.' Conspicuously absent from that list is Anthropic, which has been locked in a legal and ethical dispute with the Trump administration over the use of AI in warfare. The new testing pact builds on 2024 agreements with OpenAI and Anthropic under the Biden administration, when CAISI was known as the U.S. Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute. The center has already completed more than 40 evaluations, including on unreleased models with safety guardrails stripped back to expose vulnerabilities. The urgency is fueled by the recent unveiling of Anthropic's Mythos model, which lawmakers fear could give hackers unprecedented capabilities. By securing early access, officials aim to identify threats ranging from cyberattacks to military misuse before the tools are widely deployed. Microsoft's stock dipped 0.6% on the news, while Alphabet rose 1.3%. xAI, which is privately held, did not comment.
why_it_matters: This deal highlights a crucial tension in tech: the same AI that can help doctors or teachers could also be weaponized. For young people growing up with AI, understanding how governments and companies collaborate on safety—while balancing ethics—will shape the digital world they inherit.

background_read: CAISI, part of the Commerce Department, was originally launched as the U.S. Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute in 2024 under President Biden to evaluate AI risks before models are widely released.
Elon Musk's xAI developed Grok, a chatbot known for its candid and sometimes controversial responses, and now joins more established firms in the government pact.

Anthropic, founded by former OpenAI employees, has positioned itself as a safety-first company—its Claude model is used by millions—and it has clashed with the Trump administration over military AI use.
The Pentagon's separate agreement with seven tech giants includes integrating AI into real-time battlefield analysis, a move that critics worry could lead to autonomous weapons decisions.
Lawmakers' fears about the Mythos model echo past alarms with previous AI releases, such as GPT-4, where rapid capability increases outpaced safety measures.

perspectives.description: Proponents argue that pre-release vetting is a smart, proactive step that could stop malicious uses of AI before they happen, making everyone safer from cyber threats. Cooperation between industry and government may set a global standard for responsible AI development.

Critics worry that granting the military access to cutting-edge AI normalizes a surveillance and autonomous weapons race. Anthropic’s refusal to join the Pentagon deal reflects fears that ethical red lines will be crossed, and that unaccountable algorithms could make life-or-death decisions.

Throughout history, powerful technologies—from nuclear fission to the internet—have had both civilian and military applications. This agreement is another chapter in that story, where the same AI that accelerates discovery can also be repurposed for conflict, forcing societies to constantly renegotiate the boundary.

Looking ahead, experts say this testing pact could lead to an international treaty or institution for AI safety, much like nuclear arms control. The absence of a unified approach risks a fragmented world where some countries race ahead without guardrails, making accidents or misuse more likely.
